abstract.title: Abstract:
abstract.p: Several meta-analyses have investigated the effects of different doses of colchicine in treating coronary artery disease, but all dosing regimens were never compared in a single study. We aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of 3 dosing regimens of colchicine in patients with coronary artery disease. PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, and SCOPUS were searched for randomized controlled trials involving different colchicine doses. Major adverse cardiac events (MACE), all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, recurrent myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, gastrointestinal adverse events (AEs), discontinuation, and hospitalization were evaluated using risk ratio (RR) with 95% confidence interval (CI). A total of 15 randomized controlled trial involving 13,539 patients were included. Pooled results calculated with STATA 14.0 showed that low-dose colchicine significantly reduced MACE (RR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.32–0.83), recurrent MI (RR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.35–0.89), stroke (RR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.23–1.00), and hospitalization (RR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.22–0.85), whereas high and loading doses significantly increased gastrointestinal AEs (RR, 2.84; 95% CI, 1.26–6.24) and discontinuation (RR, 2.73; 95% CI, 1.07–6.93), respectively. Sensitivity analyses confirmed that 3 dosing regimens did not reduce all-cause and cardiovascular mortality but significantly increased the gastrointestinal AEs, and high dose significantly increased AEs-related discontinuation; loading dose resulted in more discontinuation than low dose. Although differences between 3 dosing regimens of colchicine are not significant, low dose is more effective in reducing MACE, recurrent MI, stroke, and hospitalization than the control, whereas high and loading doses increase gastrointestinal AEs and discontinuation, respectively.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains the leading cause of mortality worldwide, although several breakthroughs in optimal medical therapy.1 Inflammation is crucial to the development and progression of CAD2,3; therefore, the prevention and treatment of CAD can theoretically benefit from a therapeutic strategy targeting proinflammatory cytokines.4,5 So, it makes sense to find an effective and safe drugs for the treatment of CAD from older drugs targeting inflammation.

As an ancient anti-inflammatory drug,6,7 colchicine can affect multiple functions of inflammatory cells, such as chemotaxis and adhesion,8,9 and therefore, it has been extensively used for various rheumatic disorders (eg, acute gout, Behcet illness, and familial Mediterranean fever) and cardiac inflammatory disorders (eg, pericarditis).10,11 In recent years, colchicine has been shown to inhibit the NLRP3 inflammasome in various ways, thereby potentially benefiting patients with CAD.12,13 Thus, colchicine has emerged as a promising strategy to prevent and treat CAD because it may reduce the risk of myocardial infarction (MI) and other cardiac outcomes.14–16

Clinical studies have evaluated the efficacy and safety of colchicine on patients with CAD and identified possible benefits such as a reduction in ischemia events.14,16–18 Moreover, several meta-analyses have also confirmed the role of colchicine in patients with CAD.19–25 However, multiple colchicine doses are used in practice, including low dose (0.5 mg once daily), high dose (1.0 mg once daily or 0.5 mg twice daily), and loading dose (initial dose plus a subsequent loading dose), and the optimal dose has been debated.19,25,26 Therefore, this study used network meta-analysis to comprehensively evaluate the comparative efficacy and safety of 3 dosing regimens of colchicine in patients with CAD.

sec.title: Protocol and Registration
sec.p: The current network meta-analysis was performed and reported strictly in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Project for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis for Network Meta-analyses checklist,27 as shown in Supplemental Digital Content (see Table 1, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A948). The protocol for this network meta-analysis was prospectively registered with CRD (42022376137). Moreover, the institutional ethical approval and informed consent from patients were not required for this network meta-analysis because only published studies were included in the final data analysis.

sec.title: Information Sources
sec.p: We systematically searched 4 electronic databases including PubMed, EMBASE, the Cochrane library, and SCOPUS for retrieving potentially eligible randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Meanwhile, we also screened the references of both topic-related reviews and the included studies for finding additional studies.

sec.title: Search Strategy
sec.p: We developed specific search strategy for each database using the following medical subject heading (Mesh) and the corresponding keywords: “coronary artery disease,” “coronary heart disease,” “coronary atherosclerosis,” and “colchicine.” The literature search was limited from the establishment date of each database through October 9, 2022. Detailed search strategy of each database can be accessed in Supplemental Digital Content (see Table 2, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A949).

sec.title: Inclusion Criteria
sec.p: Eligible studies were identified based on the following criteria: (1) population: studies enrolled only adult patients diagnosed with CAD; (2) interventions: studies compared colchicine with control or compared different dosing regimens of colchicine; (3) outcomes: studies reported at least 1 of the outcomes, including major adverse cardiac events (MACE), all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, recurrent MI, stroke, hospitalization, discontinuation, and gastrointestinal adverse events (AEs); and (4) study design: RCTs published in full texts.

sec.title: Exclusion Criteria
sec.p: We excluded ineligible studies based on the following criteria: (1) studies used ineligible designs, such as case reports, observational studies, in vitro studies, or nonrandomized studies; (2) studies enrolled patients diagnosed with other cardiovascular diseases, such as atrial fibrillation, pericarditis, or heart failure; (3) conference abstracts without sufficient raw data; (4) full texts with insufficient raw data or with obviously wrong data; and (5) repeated published studies with relatively low quality and insufficient data.

sec.title: Study Selection
sec.p: Study selection was performed in 3 steps by 2 independent authors (S.W. and Y.M.). The 2 authors first used EndNote X9 to exclude duplicate published studies. Then, they screened the titles and abstracts of the remaining studies to select potential studies. Finally, they screened the full texts of all potential studies according to inclusion and exclusion criteria to identify studies eligible for this network meta-analysis. Any disagreements between the 2 authors were resolved by consensus through discussion.

sec.title: Data Extraction
sec.p: Two independent authors (L.T. and J.H.) worked for data extraction, and they used a predesigned data extraction sheet to extract the following essential data, including the name of the first author, publication year, country, study design, the details of interventions, sample size, mean age of patients, the proportion of male patients, types of diseases, the number of patients with diabetes mellitus, and the duration of follow-up. We extracted the time point data of the last follow-up as the statistical data source according to the relevant statistical theories.28 If incomplete or unclear information was occurred in the included studies, we will email the corresponding author to obtain the relevant data whenever possible.

sec.title: Outcomes Measures
sec.p: We designed MACE and all-cause mortality as the primary outcomes and cardiovascular mortality, recurrent MI, stroke, hospitalization, gastrointestinal AEs, and discontinuation from gastrointestinal AEs as the secondary outcomes. MACE was mainly defined as a composite of cardiovascular mortality, MI, ischemic stroke, or revascularization; however, the current network meta-analysis accepted different definitions of MACE. Other outcomes were defined by individual studies.

sec.title: Evidence Plot
sec.p: We produced evidence plot to describe the evidence structure for each outcome. Specifically, in each evidence plot, circles indicated interventions and solid line indicated direct comparisons between the 2 interventions. The cumulative sample size was proportional to the size of circle, and the number of direct comparisons was proportional to the width of solid line.29

sec.title: Risk of Bias Assessment
sec.p: Two authors (S.W. and J.H.) independently assessed the risk of bias of included studies using the revised Cochrane risk of bias assessment tool from the following 5 domains: randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported results.30 Each domain was rated as low, some concerns, no information, or high risk according to the matched level between actual information and assessment criteria. Overall quality was rated as high risk if at least 1 domain is rated as “high” risk, overall quality is rated as some concerns if at least 1 domain was rated as “some concerns” or “no information,” and overall quality was rated as low risk if all domains were rated as “low” risk. Disagreements between the 2 authors (S.W. and J.H.) were resolved by consensus through discussion. We used the Risk-of-Bias Visualization (robvis) to graphically depict the assessment results.31

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: All outcomes assessed in this network meta-analysis were dichotomous variables, so pooled results were expressed as risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We first performed pairwise meta-analysis to separately evaluate the efficacy and safety of each dose regimens of colchicine for the treatment of CAD.32 Statistical heterogeneity between studies was evaluated using the Cochrane Q and Higgin inconsistency factors (I2 statistic).33 If P < 0.1 and I2 > 50%, test for statistical heterogeneity was significant. Nevertheless, random-effects model was used for meta-analysis because variations in some aspects, such as study design and disease type, did exist between the studies. We performed transitivity assessment by examining the distribution of the 7 major factors across comparisons34,35 and then determined criteria for designing subgroup analyses based on the results of the transitivity assessments. In addition, variables that did not evenly distribute between various dosing regimens were regarded as covariates, and a network meta-regression was performed using self-programmed routines with the “gemtc” package36 to assess the impact of covariates on the pooled results. We performed random network meta-analysis within Bayesian framework to evaluate comparative efficacy and safety of different dose regimens of colchicine.37 Notably, we selected the consistency model for this network meta-analysis because the obtained evidence plots lacked closed loops.38,39 After calculating relative values of different dose regimens of colchicine, we produced interval forest plot to graphically display results.40 The difference between the 2 regimens was considered insignificant if the invalid vertical line intersected the horizontal line for the 95% CI. We calculated the surface under the cumulative ranking (SUCRA) curve to rank different regimens.41 Higher value of SUCRA indicated better efficacy and safety of the regimen.42 Loop inconsistency examination was not conducted because closed loop was not available.43,44 Finally, publication bias was tested using comparison-adjusted funnel plot,45 Egger test,46 and Begg test.47 Network meta-analysis was performed using Stata 14.0 (StataCorp LP, College Station, TX) with “network” command.48

sec.title: Literature Selection
sec.p: A total of 911 records were retrieved from our initial literature search, of which 290 records were excluded for duplicate records and registries and 598 records were excluded by title and abstract screening. Therefore, we accessed the full texts of the remaining 23 articles for eligibility assessment, of which 1 study was excluded because it was a meta-analysis, 4 studies were excluded because only included ineligible outcomes, 1 study was excluded because it was not published in English, and 2 studies were excluded because of unrelating to our topic. Finally, 15 studies14–18,49–58 were included in this network meta-analysis. Figure 1 depicts the process for selecting studies and reasons for excluding studies.

sec.title: Characteristics of the Included Studies
sec.p: Of the 15 eligible studies, 6 studies14–16,49,53,54 evaluated low dose, 6 studies17,18,51,52,55,56 evaluated high dose, and 3 studies50,57,58 evaluated loading dose. The sample size of each study ranged between 44 and 5522, with an accumulated number of 13,539. Ten studies14–17,49,53,54,56–58 reported MACE, 14 studies14–18,49–53,55–58 reported all-cause mortality, 11 studies14–17,49–51,53,54,56,58 reported cardiovascular mortality, 9 studies14–17,49,53,54,57,58 reported recurrent MI, 8 studies14–16,51,54,56–58 reported stroke, 5 studies15,16,53,56,58 reported hospitalization, 14 studies14–17,49–58 reported gastrointestinal AEs, and 11 studies14–17,50–53,55,56,58 reported discontinuation due to gastrointestinal AEs. Table 1 summarizes the basic characteristics of the included studies, Supplemental Digital Content (see Table 3, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A950) documents the outcomes of the 15 eligible studies, and Supplemental Digital Content (see Figure 1, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A941) describes the evidence structure for each outcome.

sec.title: Risk of Bias of Eligible Studies
sec.p: In all eligible studies, 1 study18 did not perform allocation concealment and 1 study55 used inappropriate approach to perform allocation concealment, so the 2 studies were therefore rated as “high” risk and “some concerns,” respectively. Two studies18,51 did not blind participants, and 1 study53 did not report information on whether participants and personnel were blinded or not, so 2 studies were therefore rated as “high” risk and 1 study was therefore rated as “no information.” All studies14–18,49–58 did not miss outcome data and were therefore rated as “low” risk. Three studies17,18,56 did not blind outcome assessors and were therefore rated as “high” risk, and 3 studies53–55 did not report information on whether outcome were assessed by blinded assessors or not and were therefore rated as “no information.” All studies14–18,49–58 reported anticipated outcomes and were therefore rated as “low” risk. Finally, the overall quality of 4 studies were rated as “high” risk, 3 studies were rated as “some concerns,” and 8 studies were rated as “low” risk. Detailed results of the risk of bias assessment are depicted in Supplemental Digital Content (see Figure 2, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A942).

sec.title: Transitivity Assessment
sec.p: As shown in Supplemental Digital Content (see Table 4, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A951), year of publication, sample size, proportion of male patients, mean age of patients, and number of diabetic patients were evenly distributed among the different comparisons. However, there were significant differences in the distribution of disease types and duration of follow-up within 2 comparisons, including comparison of low versus high doses and comparison of high versus loading doses.

sec.title: Meta-analysis of MACE
sec.p: Pairwise meta-analysis based on subgroup analysis showed that only low-dose colchicine significantly reduced MACE (RR, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.35–0.79; I2 = 72.8%; P = 0.002 for the test of effect size; see Figure 3, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A943). Network meta-analysis consistently revealed the therapeutic efficacy of low dose in reducing MACE (RR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.32–0.83) and did not change the results of the other 2 dose regimens (Fig. 2). However, the network meta-analysis did not reveal differences between the 3 dosing regimens of colchicine (Fig. 2).

sec.title: Meta-analysis of the All-cause Mortality
sec.p: Pairwise meta-analysis based on subgroup analysis showed that 3 dosing regimens of colchicine did not reduce all-cause mortality (see Figure 3, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A943), as confirmed by the results of network meta-analysis (Fig. 2). Furthermore, the network meta-analysis did not also reveal differences between the 3 dosing regimens of colchicine (Fig. 2).

sec.title: Meta-analysis of Cardiovascular Mortality
sec.p: Pairwise meta-analysis based on subgroup analysis showed that 3 dosing regimens of colchicine did not reduce cardiovascular mortality (see Figure 4, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A944), as confirmed by the results of network meta-analysis (Fig. 3). Furthermore, the network meta-analysis did not also reveal differences between the 3 dosing regimens of colchicine (Fig. 3).

caption.p: Network meta-analysis of cardiovascular mortality, recurrent MI, stroke, gastrointestinal AEs, discontinuation due to AEs, and hospitalization.

sec.title: Meta-analysis of Recurrent MI
sec.p: Pairwise meta-analysis based on subgroup analysis showed that only low dose significantly reduced recurrent MI (RR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.24–0.96; I2 = 25.6%; P = 0.006 for the test of effect size; see Figure 4, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A944). Network meta-analysis consistently revealed the therapeutic efficacy of low dose in reducing recurrent MI (RR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.35–0.89) and did not change the results of the other 2 dosing regimens (Fig. 3). However, the network meta-analysis did not reveal differences between the 3 dosing regimens of colchicine (Fig. 3).

sec.title: Meta-analysis of Stroke
sec.p: Pairwise meta-analysis based on subgroup analysis showed that only low dose significantly reduced stroke (RR, 0.57; 95% CI, 0.38–0.85; I2 = 64.6%; P = 0.039 for the test of effect size; see Figure 4, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A944). Network meta-analysis consistently revealed the therapeutic efficacy of low dose in reducing recurrent stroke (RR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.23–1.00) and did not change the results of the other 2 dosing regimens (Fig. 3). However, the network meta-analysis did not reveal differences between the 3 dosing regimens of colchicine (Fig. 3).

sec.title: Meta-analysis of Gastrointestinal AEs
sec.p: Pairwise meta-analysis based on subgroup analysis showed that only high dose significantly increased the risk of gastrointestinal AEs (RR, 2.50; 95% CI, 1.62–3.84; I2 = 0.00%; P < 0.001 for the test of effect size; see Figure 4, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A944). Network meta-analysis consistently revealed the risk of high dose in increasing gastrointestinal AEs (RR, 2.84; 95% CI, 1.26–6.42) and did not change the results of the other 2 dosing regimens (Fig. 3). However, the network meta-analysis did not reveal differences between the 3 dosing regimens of colchicine (Fig. 3).

sec.title: Meta-analysis of Discontinuation Due to AEs
sec.p: Pairwise meta-analysis based on subgroup analysis showed that only high dose significantly increased discontinuation (RR, 2.03; 95% CI, 1.12–3.69; I2 = 0.00%; P < 0.020 for the test of effect size; see Figure 4, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A944); however, network meta-analysis significantly changed the results of pairwise meta-analysis and revealed that loading dose was associated with significantly increased discontinuation (RR, 2.73; 95% CI, 1.07–6.93; Fig. 3). However, the network meta-analysis did not reveal differences between the 3 dosing regimens of colchicine (Fig. 3).

sec.title: Meta-analysis of the Hospitalization
sec.p: Pairwise meta-analysis based on subgroup analysis showed that only low dose significantly reduced the risk of hospitalization (RR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.22–0.87; I2 = 85.4%; P = 0.018 for the test of effect size; see Figure 4, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A944). Network meta-analysis consistently revealed the therapeutic efficacy of low dose in reducing the risk of hospitalization (RR, 0.44; 95% CI, 0.22–0.85) and did not change the results of the other 2 dosing regimens (Fig. 3). However, the network meta-analysis did not reveal differences between the 3 dosing regimens of colchicine (Fig. 3).

sec.title: Sensitivity Analysis
sec.p: Based on the results of the transitivity assessment, disease type and follow-up duration were found to have significantly different distributions between the comparisons. Therefore, we conducted sensitivity analyses by excluding studies that enrolled patients with different types of disease and studies that designed long follow-up period. As shown in Supplemental Digital Content (see Figure 5, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A945), sensitivity analyses revealed that low dose was associated with a significantly lower gastrointestinal AEs (RR, 0.02; 95% CI, 0.00–0.51) after excluding studies that included patients with different types of disease. As shown in Supplemental Digital Content (see Figure 6, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A946), sensitivity analyses by excluding studies that designed long follow-up period consistently revealed that low dose significantly reduced MACE and recurrent MI, but it also showed that 3 dosing regimens of colchicine are all associated with an increased risk of gastrointestinal AEs, high and loading dose significantly increased discontinuation, and loading dose resulted in a significantly higher discontinuation than low dose (RR, 12.59; 95% CI, 1.63–97.32).

sec.title: Network Meta-regression
sec.p: As described previously, disease type and follow-up duration did not evenly distribute between 3 dosing regimens and therefore were regarded as covariates. The results of the network meta-regressions, as shown in Supplemental Digital Content (see Table 5, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A952), showed that these 2 potential effect modifiers did not have negative effect on the pooled results because all 95% CIs covered zero.

sec.title: Ranking Probabilities
sec.p: The SUCRA plots for all outcomes are shown in Figures 4 and 5. Specifically, for MACE, low dose had the highest probability 80.7%, followed by loading dose (61.2%) and high dose (37.6%). For all-cause mortality and recurrent MI, high dose had the highest probability of 90.7% and 68.7%, followed by low dose (42.9% and 62.6%) and loading dose (8.6% and 55.1%). For cardiovascular mortality, low dose had the highest probability of 73.4%, followed by high dose (54.9%) and loading dose (24.1%). For stroke, low dose ranked first, with a probability of 73.1%, followed by loading dose (66.4%) and high dose (37.0). For gastrointestinal AEs, low dose ranked the best, with a ranking probability of 48.8%, followed by loading dose (32.69%) and high dose (21.8%). For discontinuation due to gastrointestinal AEs, low dose ranked first (65.2%), followed by high dose (28.2%) and loading dose (15.2%). For hospitalization, loading dose had the highest probability of 73.9%, followed by low dose (69.3%) and high dose (34.0%).

sec.title: Publication Bias
sec.p: As shown in Supplemental Digital Content (see Figure 7, http://links.lww.com/JCVP/A947), comparison-adjusted funnel plots were used to visually check for publication bias. All studies were symmetrically distributed in funnel plots for MACE, all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, recurrent MI, stroke, discontinuation, and hospitalization, suggesting no apparent publication bias for these outcomes. However, studies were asymmetrically distributed in the funnel plot of gastrointestinal AEs, indicating publication bias. Furthermore, quantitative examination revealed no publication bias for MACE (Egger test: P = 0.093, Begg test: P = 0.586), cardiovascular mortality (Egger test: P = 0.952, Begg test: P = 0.602), recurrent MI (Egger test: P = 0.099, Begg test: P = 0.31), stroke (Egger test: P = 0.848, Begg test: P = 0.540), discontinuation (Egger test: P = 0.056, Begg test: P = 0.173), and hospitalization (Egger test: P = 0.925, Begg test: P = 0.73). However, publication bias was detected for all-cause mortality (Egger test: P < 0.001, Begg test: P = 0.566) and gastrointestinal AEs (Egger test: P < 0.001, Begg test: P = 0.010).

sec.title: Main Findings
sec.p: Although colchicine has been shown to be beneficial in the treatment of CAD, it is unclear which dosing regimen of colchicine may be the best treatment option. In this current network meta-analysis, we are the first to compare the efficacy and safety of 3 dosing regimens of colchicine in the treatment of patients with CAD. The final data analysis included 15 eligible RCTs involving 13,539 patients, and pooled results showed that low-dose colchicine significantly reduced MACE, recurrent MI, stroke, and hospitalization, but high dose significantly increased gastrointestinal AEs, and loading dose significantly increased discontinuation due to AEs. Sensitivity analyses further confirmed that none of the 3 dosing regimens reduced all-cause and cardiovascular mortalities but significantly increased gastrointestinal AEs. Furthermore, sensitivity analyses showed that high dose significantly increased discontinuation due to AEs, whereas loading dose resulted in more discontinuation due to AEs than low dose.

sec.title: Interpretation of Findings
sec.p: The current network meta-analysis showed that low dose of colchicine had significant benefits on clinical outcomes of patients with CAD. As an old drug with broad anti-inflammatory impact,58 colchicine does not only target the NACHT, leucine-rich repeat, and pyrin domain–containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome, a new important therapeutic target for myopericardial diseases, to cause the upregulation of IL-1 and IL-6 downstream59 but also disrupts microtubules to exert antimitotic effects.60 In addition, colchicine is also regarded as benefiting the treatment of cardiovascular illness by suppressing cholesterol crystals within atherosclerotic plaques. All these mechanisms provide a potential explanation of why colchicine can benefit CAD.61 All these mechanisms provide a potential explanation on why colchicine can benefit CAD. Ranking probability revealed that low dose may be better than another 2 dosing regimens, although the differences between different doses did not achieve statistical significance in the efficacy. Notably, colchicine has a narrow therapeutic window, and actually, adverse effects related to the administration of colchicine have been extensively evaluated.62 A previous meta-analysis has also revealed a significant association between the administration of colchicine and AEs and suggested that higher dose was harder to be intolerable.63 Undoubtedly, the adverse effects caused by higher dose will compromise its therapeutic benefits, therefore leading to the result that higher dose is inferior to lower dose in the therapeutic efficacy. Thus, based on the possible mechanisms of colchicine in exerting anti-inflammation, it is rational to extend the usage of colchicine from secondary prevention to primary prevention for cardiovascular diseases, especially low dose of colchicine64; however, this hypothesis should be evaluated by future studies, such as an ongoing study registered on ClinicalTrials.gov.65

Although our network meta-analysis suggested a significantly lower risk of recurrent MI in patients receiving low dose of colchicine and a numerically lower risk in cardioembolic stroke. We are not surprised with these results because MI, especially acute MI, has been a long-established risk factor for ischemic stroke.66,67 Nevertheless, such benefits were not attributed to a mortality benefit in this network meta-analysis, which was consistent with the findings of previous meta-analyses.20,63,68 It should not be ignored that various disease types were evaluated in eligible studies, therefore inevitably introducing bias to compromise mortality benefit. Moreover, we cannot also eliminate the influence of variations in follow-up durations on mortality. Therefore, the effect of the low dose of colchicine on mortality should be further evaluated in future studies.

sec.title: The Strengths of This Network Meta-analysis
sec.p: To date, many conventional pairwise meta-analyses have systematically evaluated and consistently established the effects and safety of colchicine for the treatment of patients with CAD19–26,63,68,69; however, all these findings from previous meta-analyses did not inform practitioners which dosing regimen may be preferred for these patients. Given this open issue, the current network meta-analysis rationally classified colchicine dose into 3 regimens based on published evidence26 and first determined the comparative efficacy and safety among 3 dosing regimens. Generally speaking, our network meta-analysis yielded these novel findings due to the following methodological advantages: (1) this network meta-analysis combined both direct and indirect evidence to evaluate the differences between the 3 dosing regimens of colchicine; (2) the current network meta-analysis meaningfully classified dose of colchicine into low, high, and loading dose rather than simply high and low dose, which was beneficial in providing more detail for clinical decision making; (3) our network meta-analysis performed sensitivity analyses based on the results of the transitivity assessment, which was beneficial to examine the robustness and reliability of our findings; (4) a network meta-regression was performed to confirm that possible effect modifiers (disease type and follow-up duration) did not have effect on the robustness of pooled results; (5) more clinical and safety outcomes were evaluated in our network meta-analysis, providing a more comprehensive profile for effect and safety of colchicine; and (6) SUCRA values were calculated to rank the 3 dosing regimens of colchicine, which can help in developing the correct treatment strategy.

sec.title: Limitations of This Network Meta-analysis
sec.p: Although our findings fill a gap caused by the lack of direct comparisons of different doses of colchicine in patients with CAD, the current network meta-analysis should be interpreted with caution due to the following limitations. First, all eligible RCTs have their own limitations, and using meta-analysis to pool them together inevitably limits the robustness of data interpretation. Second, the final follow-up time point of some outcomes in some studies was inconsistent, which may have a certain impact on the relevant outcome indicators. In fact, transitivity assessment confirmed this issue, so we performed sensitivity analysis according to follow-up periods to exam the impact of follow-up periods on the pooled results. Third, the current network meta-analysis did not include unpublished data or articles published in other languages. Fourth, the definitions of MACE varied across trials, so all components of this outcome were analyzed separately. Fifth, most of the included RCTs were conducted in Western countries and lack data on Asians, which may have contributed to bias. Sixth, whereas the transitivity assessment was based on 7 main factors, other potentially important factors could not be assessed in the current network because most eligible studies did not report relevant information. Finally, we did not publicly register a formal protocol for the current network meta-analysis; however, the reliability of our findings would not be compromised because we performed all procedures strictly as recommended in the Cochrane Handbook.

sec.title: CONCLUSIONS
sec.p: This network meta-analysis showed that among the 3 dosing regimens of colchicine, although the difference between the 3 dosing regimens was not significant, low dose was the best option for the treatment of patients with CAD compared with the control group because it benefits reducing MACE, recurrent MI, stroke, and hospitalization, whereas high dose increases gastrointestinal AEs and loading dose increases discontinuation. However, considering the limitations of this network meta-analysis, more high-quality RCTs should be conducted in the future to further confirm the current findings.
